replacement: 4. But someone may say that the senses occasionally mislead us about small objects, or about things too far away to examine closely, yet many other things they report (presentations) cannot manifestly be doubted. For example, that I am in this place, seated by the fire, wearing a winter dressing gown, holding this piece of paper in my hands, and other things of the same kind. But how could I deny that these hands and this body are mine? I would have to count myself among the insane, whose brains are so disordered and clouded by dark bilious vapors that they stubbornly insist they are kings when they are in the greatest poverty, or that they are dressed [in gold] and purple when they have nothing on, or that their head is made of clay, their body of glass, or that they are gourds. But these people are madmen, and I would be no less insane than they if I took such extravagant examples as my guide.

10. Some people, indeed, might perhaps be found who would rather deny the existence of so powerful a Being than believe that nothing is certain. But for the present let us not oppose this view, and let us grant that everything said here about a Deity is fable. Still, however it is supposed that I came to be what I am, whether by fate, or chance, or an endless series of antecedents and consequents, or any other means, being deceived and being in error are a certain defect. So it is clear that the probability of my being so imperfect as to be constantly deceived increases exactly as the power of the cause assigned as my origin decreases. To these arguments I have assuredly nothing to reply. I am forced at last to admit that there is nothing among all I formerly believed true that it is impossible to doubt, and this not through thoughtlessness or levity but for cogent and carefully considered reasons. So from now on, if I want to discover anything certain, I should withhold assent from those same opinions just as carefully as from what could be shown to be manifestly false.

11. But it is not enough to have made these observations. I must also take care to remember them. For those old, customary opinions keep coming back. Long and familiar use gives them the right to occupy my mind, even almost against my will, and to take control of my belief. I will not lose the habit of deferring to them and trusting them so long as I consider them what they truly are, namely, opinions that are to some extent doubtful, as I have already shown, but still highly probable, and that it is much more reasonable to believe than to deny. For this reason I am persuaded that I will not be doing wrong if, deliberately taking the opposite judgment, I become my own deceiver. I will suppose for a time that all those opinions are entirely false and imaginary, until at length I have balanced my old prejudices against my new ones, and my judgment is no longer turned aside by distorted habit from the path that may lead to the perception of truth. For I am assured that in the meantime this course will bring neither danger nor error, and that I cannot for now yield too much to distrust, since the end I am seeking is not action but knowledge.

6. But [as for myself, what can I now say that I am], since I suppose there is an extremely powerful and, if I may say so, malignant being whose whole effort is directed to deceiving me? Can I affirm that I have any one of the attributes I have just described as belonging to the nature of body? I consider them attentively in my own mind, and I find none of them that can properly be said to belong to me. To list them would be idle and tedious. Let us pass, then, to the attributes of the soul. The first named were nutrition and walking. But if it is true that I have no body, it is also true that I can neither walk nor be nourished. Perception is another attribute of the soul. But perception too is impossible without the body. Besides, I have often believed in sleep that I perceived things which I afterward saw I had not really perceived. Thinking is another attribute of the soul, and here I find what properly belongs to me. This alone cannot be separated from me. I am — I exist: this is certain. But how often? As often as I think. For perhaps it could even happen, if I wholly ceased to think, that I would at the same time wholly cease to be. I now admit nothing that is not necessarily true. Precisely speaking, then, I am only a thinking thing, that is, a mind (mens sive animus), understanding, or reason, terms whose meaning I did not know before. Yet I am a real thing, and really exist. But what thing? I have answered: a thinking thing.

10. From this I begin to know what I am a little more clearly and distinctly than before. But it still seems to me, and I cannot help believing, that corporeal things, whose images are formed by thought [which fall under the senses] and are examined by thought, are known much more distinctly than that part of myself, I know not what, which cannot be imagined. It may indeed seem strange to say that I know and comprehend more distinctly things whose existence appears doubtful to me, which are unknown and do not belong to me, than things of whose reality I am persuaded, which are known to me and belong to my own nature. In a word, it seems strange to say that I know them more distinctly than I know myself. But I see clearly what is happening. My mind likes to wander, and will not yet submit to being held within the limits of truth. Let us therefore leave the mind to itself once more, and give it every kind of liberty [to consider the objects that appear to it from outside], so that, having drawn it away from these gently and at the right moment [and fixed it on the consideration of its being and the properties it finds in itself], it may then be more easily controlled.

13. Meanwhile, I am greatly astonished when I observe [the weakness of my mind and] how prone it is to error. For although I consider all this silently in my own mind, without giving any expression to what I think, words still sometimes get in my way, and I am almost led into error by the terms of ordinary language. We say, for example, that we see the same wax when it is before us, and not that we judge it to be the same because it keeps the same color and figure. From this I would immediately be inclined to conclude that the wax is known by the act of sight and not by the intuition of the mind alone, were it not for a similar case: human beings passing in the street below, as seen from a window. In this case I do not hesitate to say that I see the men themselves, just as I say that I see the wax. Yet what do I see from the window besides hats and cloaks, which might cover artificial machines moved by springs? But from these appearances I judge that they are human beings. And so I comprehend, by the faculty of judgment alone which is in my mind, what I believed I saw with my eyes.

1. I will now close my eyes, stop my ears and turn my senses away from their objects. I will even wipe from my consciousness all the images of corporeal things; or, since that can hardly be done, I will at least regard them as empty and false. Holding conversation only with myself and examining my nature closely, I will try to gain, step by step, a more intimate and familiar knowledge of myself. I am a thinking (conscious) thing, that is, a being who doubts, affirms, denies, knows a few things and is ignorant of many — [who loves, hates], wills, refuses, and who also imagines and perceives. For, as I remarked before, the things I perceive or imagine are perhaps nothing at all apart from me [and in themselves]; yet I am assured that those modes of consciousness I call perceptions and imaginations exist in me, but only insofar as they are modes of consciousness.

11. And finally, even if I granted that they proceeded from those objects, it does not necessarily follow that they must be like them. On the contrary, I have observed in many cases a great difference between the object and its idea. For example, I find in my mind two wholly different ideas of the sun. One, by which it appears extremely small, derives from the senses and should be placed among adventitious ideas. The other, by which it seems many times larger than the whole earth, is adopted on astronomical grounds, that is, drawn out of certain notions born with me, or else framed by myself in some other way. These two ideas certainly cannot both resemble the same sun; and reason teaches me that the one which seems to have come most directly from it is the most unlike.

21. Among the clear and distinct ideas of corporeal things, there are some which, as it appears to me, might have been taken from the idea I have of myself: those of substance, duration, number and the like. When I think that a stone is a substance, or a thing capable of existing of itself, and that I am also a substance, I conceive that I am a thinking and non-extended thing and that the stone, on the contrary, is extended and unconscious, so that there is the greatest diversity between the two concepts; yet these two ideas seem to have this in common, that they both represent substances. In the same way, when I think of myself as existing now, recall that I existed some time ago, and am conscious of various thoughts whose number I know, I acquire the ideas of duration and number, which I can afterward transfer to as many objects as I please. As for the other qualities that make up the ideas of corporeal objects, namely extension, figure, situation and motion, it is true that they are not in me formally, since I am merely a thinking being. But because they are only certain modes of substance, and I myself am a substance, it seems possible that they may be contained in me eminently.

31. Nor would it help to suppose that I have always been as I am now: that would not let me escape these reasonings, because even then it would not follow that I need not look for an author of my existence. For the whole span of my life divides into infinitely many parts, and none of them depends on any other. So the fact that I existed a little while ago does not mean I must exist now, unless some cause creates me afresh at this moment, so to speak, that is, conserves me. Anyone who attentively considers the nature of duration will see perfectly clearly that a substance needs the same power and the same act to be conserved at each moment of its duration as it would need to be created if it did not yet exist. It is therefore manifestly a dictate of the natural light that conservation and creation differ only in our mode of thinking [and not in reality].

35. Nor can we suppose that several causes together produced me, so that I got the idea of one perfection I attribute to Deity from one cause and the idea of another from another, and that all those perfections are found somewhere in the universe but not all together in a single being, God. The reverse is the case: the unity, simplicity and inseparability of all the properties of Deity is itself one of the chief perfections I conceive him to have. The idea of this unity of all the perfections of Deity could certainly not have been put in my mind by a cause from which I had not also received the ideas of all the other perfections. For no power could make me grasp them in one inseparable unity without also giving me knowledge of what they were [and of their existence in a particular mode].

37. It remains only to ask how I received this idea from God, for I did not draw it from the senses, and it does not come upon me unexpectedly, as ideas of sensible objects usually do when these objects are presented, or seem to be presented, to the external sense organs. Nor is it merely something my mind made up or invented, since I cannot take anything away from it or add anything to it. The only alternative left, then, is that it is innate, as the idea of myself is.

39. Before I examine this more attentively and move on to other truths that can be drawn from it, I think it right to stay here for a while and contemplate God himself — to ponder his marvelous attributes at leisure, and to behold, admire and adore the beauty of this light so unspeakably great, as far, at least, as the strength of my mind, somewhat dazzled by the sight, will permit. For just as we learn by faith that the supreme felicity of the next life lies in contemplating the Divine majesty alone, so we learn from experience even now that a similar meditation, though incomparably less perfect, gives the highest satisfaction we are capable of in this life.

5. Still, this does not yet fully satisfy me. For error is not a pure negation, [in other words, not just the lack of some knowledge that is not owed to me]; it is a privation, the lack of some knowledge that it seems I ought to have. Yet when I think about the nature of God, it seems impossible that he would have planted in his creature a faculty not perfect of its kind, that is, one lacking a perfection that is due to it; for if it is true that the more skillful the maker, the more perfect his work, what could the supreme Creator of the universe have made that is not absolutely perfect in all its parts? And surely there is no doubt that God could have created me so that I would never be deceived; it is also certain that he always wills what is best. Is it better, then, for me to be capable of being deceived than not to be?

7. It also strikes me that, to judge the perfection of the works of Deity, we should not look at one creature in isolation but at all his creatures together. For something that might perhaps, with some show of reason, seem highly imperfect if it were alone in the world may still be the most perfect possible when seen as a part of the whole universe. It was my purpose to doubt everything, and so far I know with certainty only my own existence and God's. Nevertheless, having noted the infinite power of Deity, I cannot deny that he may have produced many other objects, or at least that he is able to produce them, so that I have a place as a part in relation to the great whole of his creatures.

8. Now I look at myself more closely and ask what my errors are (which alone show that there is imperfection in me). I observe that they depend on two causes working together: the faculty of cognition I have, and the faculty of election or power of free choice — in other words, the understanding and the will. For by the understanding alone I [neither affirm nor deny anything but] merely apprehend (percipio) the ideas about which I can form a judgment, and when it is taken precisely in this way, no error properly so called is found in it. There are perhaps countless objects in the world of which I have no idea in my understanding. Still, it cannot be said that I am deprived of those ideas [as of something due to my nature]; I simply do not have them. For there is really no ground for proving that Deity ought to have given me a larger faculty of cognition than he did. However skillful a workman I take him to be, I have no reason to think he was bound to give each of his works all the perfections he can give to some. Nor can I complain that God has not given me freedom of choice, or a will ample and perfect enough, since I am conscious of a will so wide and extended that it is superior to all limits. What strikes me as highly remarkable here is that among all my other properties there is none so great and perfect that I do not clearly discern it could be greater and more perfect still. Take the faculty of understanding: I find it very small in extent and greatly limited, and yet I form the idea of another faculty of the same nature, much more ample and even infinite; and since I can frame the idea of it, I discover from that fact alone that it belongs to the nature of God. Likewise, if I examine memory or imagination or any other faculty I have, I find each one small and circumscribed, and in God immense [and infinite]. It is only the faculty of will, or freedom of choice, that I experience to be so great that I cannot conceive the idea of one more ample and extended. So it is chiefly my will that makes me discern that I bear a certain image and similitude of Deity. For although the faculty of will is incomparably greater in God than in me, both because of the knowledge and power joined with it, which make it stronger and more efficacious, and because of its object, since in him it extends to more things, it nevertheless does not appear to me greater, considered in itself formally and precisely. For the power of will consists only in this: that we are able to do or not to do the same thing (that is, to affirm or deny, to pursue or shun it); or, better, in this alone: that when we affirm or deny, pursue or shun, what the understanding proposes to us, we act without being conscious of any external force determining us to a particular action. For freedom does not require me to be equally indifferent toward each of two contraries. On the contrary, the more I incline toward one of them, whether because I clearly know that the reason of truth and goodness is in it or because God so disposes my thought from within, the more freely I choose and embrace it. Divine grace and natural knowledge, far from reducing liberty, assuredly increase and strengthen it. The indifference I am conscious of when no reason impels me to one side rather than the other is the lowest grade of liberty: it shows a defect or negation of knowledge rather than a perfection of will. For if I always clearly knew what was true and good, I would never have trouble deciding what judgment to form or what choice to make, and so I would be entirely free without ever being indifferent.

15. And finally, I should not complain that God concurs with me in forming the acts of this will, the judgments in which I am deceived, because, in so far as they depend on God, those acts are wholly true and good, and being able to form them is a higher degree of perfection in my nature than being unable would be. Privation, in which alone the formal reason of error and sin consists, needs no concurrence of Deity, because it is not a thing [or existence]; and if it is referred to God as its cause, it should be called not privation but negation [in the sense these words have in the schools]. For in truth it is no imperfection in Deity that he has given me the power to give or withhold my assent on certain matters of which he has not put a clear and distinct knowledge in my understanding. But it is doubtless an imperfection in me that I do not use my freedom rightly, and readily pass judgment on matters I conceive only obscurely and confusedly. I perceive, nevertheless, that Deity could easily have made me so that I would never be deceived while still remaining free and having limited knowledge. He could have done this by implanting in my understanding a clear and distinct knowledge of everything I would ever have to deliberate about; or simply by engraving so deeply on my memory the resolution never to judge anything without first conceiving it clearly and distinctly that I could never forget it. And I easily understand that, considering myself as a single whole, with no reference to any other being in the universe, I would have been much more perfect than I am if Deity had created me superior to error. But I cannot therefore deny that it is somehow a greater perfection in the universe for some of its parts not to be exempt from defect, as others are, than for all of them to be perfectly alike. And I have no right to complain that God, who placed me in the world, did not want me to hold that rank which is the chief and most perfect of all.

16. I even have good reason to be content. If he has not given me the perfection of being superior to error by the first means I noted above, which depends on clear and evident knowledge of everything I can deliberate about, he has at least left in my power the other means: to hold firmly to the resolution never to judge where the truth is not clearly known to me. For, although I am conscious of the weakness that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same thought, I can nevertheless, by attentive and oft-repeated meditation, impress that resolution so strongly on my memory that I will never fail to recall it when I need it, and in this way I can acquire the habit of not erring.

5. What I find most important here is this. I discover in my mind countless ideas of certain objects. These cannot be counted as pure negations, although perhaps they have no reality beyond my thought. I did not make them up, even though it may be in my power to think of them or not. They have true and immutable natures of their own. Take the example of a triangle. Perhaps there is not, and never was, any such figure anywhere in the universe outside my thought. Still, it remains true that this figure has a certain determinate nature, form or essence, which is immutable and eternal, was not made up by me, and does not depend at all on my thought. This is clear from the fact that many properties of the triangle can be demonstrated: that its three angles are equal to two right angles, that its greatest side is opposite its greatest angle, and the like. Whether I wish it or not, I now clearly discern that these belong to the triangle, although I did not think of them at all when I first imagined it. So it cannot be said that I invented them.

10. I find in myself, moreover, several faculties of thinking, each with its own special mode. I find, for example, the faculties of imagining and perceiving. I can indeed clearly and distinctly conceive myself as a whole without them. But I cannot conceive them without conceiving myself; that is, they require an intelligent substance in which they reside. For [in the notion we have of them, or to use the terms of the schools] their formal concept includes some sort of intellection. Hence I perceive that they are distinct from myself, as modes are from things. I notice certain other faculties too, such as changing place or taking on various figures. Like the preceding ones, these cannot be conceived, and so cannot exist, apart from a substance in which they inhere. It is very evident, however, that if these faculties really exist, they must belong to some corporeal or extended substance; for their clear and distinct concept contains some sort of extension, and no intellection at all. Further, I cannot doubt that I have a certain passive faculty of perception, that is, of receiving and recognizing the ideas of sensible things. But this would be useless to me unless there were also an active faculty, in me or in something else, able to form and produce those ideas. Yet this active faculty cannot be in me [insofar as I am but a thinking thing], seeing that it does not presuppose thought, and also that those ideas are often produced in my mind without any contribution from me, and even often against my will. So this faculty must exist in a substance different from me. In that substance, as I remarked before, all the objective reality of the ideas it produces is contained formally or eminently. This substance is either a body, that is, a corporeal nature that contains formally [and in effect] everything contained objectively [and by representation] in those ideas; or it is God Himself, or some other creature of a rank superior to body, that contains the same eminently. But God is no deceiver. So it is manifest that He does not send me those ideas directly from Himself, nor through any creature that contains their objective reality not formally but only eminently. For He has given me no faculty to discover that this is so. On the contrary, He has given me a very strong inclination to believe that the ideas arise from corporeal objects. I do not see how He could be cleared of deceit if they really came from some other source or were produced by other causes than corporeal things. Accordingly, it must be concluded that corporeal objects exist. They are perhaps not exactly as we perceive them by the senses, since sense perception is in many cases very obscure and confused. But at least we must admit that everything I clearly and distinctly conceive in them, that is, generally speaking everything included in the object of speculative geometry, really exists external to me.

15. There are, however, many other beliefs that seem to be taught by nature but are not. They found a place in my mind through a habit of judging things without enough consideration, and such judgments can easily contain error. Here are examples. I hold that any space where nothing affects [or makes an impression on] my senses is void. I hold that a hot body contains something in every respect similar to my idea of heat; that a white or green body contains the very whiteness or greenness I perceive; that a bitter or sweet body contains the same taste, and so on; and that the stars, towers and all distant bodies have the same size and figure as they appear to have to our eyes, etc. To avoid any indistinctness of conception, I must define precisely what I properly mean by being taught by nature. I am using nature here in a narrower sense than the sum of all that God has given me. In that wider sense the notion takes in much that belongs only to the mind [which I am not referring to here when I use the term nature]: for example, my notion of the truth that what is done cannot be undone, and all the other truths I discern by the natural light [ without the aid of the body]. It also takes in much that belongs only to body and is not included here under the name nature, such as the quality of heaviness and the like, of which I am not speaking. I keep the term exclusively for the things God has given me as a being composed of mind and body. In the sense I have explained, then, nature teaches me to shun whatever causes me the sensation of pain, and to pursue whatever gives me the sensation of pleasure, and other things of that sort. I do not find, however, that it also teaches me to draw conclusions about external objects from these diverse perceptions of the senses, unless the mind has first considered them [carefully and maturely]. For, as it appears to me, discerning the truth in such matters is the task of the mind alone, not of the composite whole of mind and body. Thus a star makes no larger an impression on my eye than the flame of a candle does. Yet I feel no real or positive impulse that determines me to believe the star is not greater than the flame. The true account is merely that I have judged so since my youth, without any rational ground. Likewise I feel heat when I approach the fire, and pain if I come too close. But this gives me no ground for holding that something resembling the heat I feel is in the fire, any more than that something similar to the pain is in it. All I have ground for believing is that the fire contains something, whatever it may be, which excites in me those sensations of heat or pain. In the same way, there are spaces where I find nothing that excites and affects my senses; but I must not therefore conclude that those spaces contain no body. For I see that here, as in many similar matters, I have been accustomed to pervert the order of nature. Nature gave me the perceptions of the senses merely to signify to my mind what is beneficial and what is hurtful to the composite whole of which it is a part, and they are clear and distinct enough for that purpose. Nevertheless I use them as infallible rules for determining at once the essence of the bodies outside me, about which they can of course give me only the most obscure and confused knowledge.

17. But we also fairly often err in what nature directly impels us to, as sick people do when they long for drink or food that would harm them. Perhaps it will be objected that such people are deceived because their nature is corrupted. That does not remove the difficulty, for a sick man is just as truly a creature of God as a healthy man, so it is equally repugnant to the goodness of God that the former's nature should be deceitful as that the latter's should be. Take a clock, made of wheels and counter weights. If it is badly made and tells the hours wrongly, it follows all the laws of nature just as accurately as when it does exactly what its maker wanted. Likewise, consider the human body as a sort of machine, built and put together from bones, nerves, muscles, veins, blood and skin. Suppose that even if it had no mind in it, it would still make all the same motions it now makes involuntarily, and so without the aid of the mind, [simply through the dispositions of its organs]. I easily see that such a body, if it were dropsical, for example, would naturally experience the parchedness of throat that is usually joined in the mind with the sensation of thirst. This parchedness would dispose it to move its nerves and other parts as drinking requires, so that it would worsen its illness and harm itself. And it is just as natural for a body that is not ill to be moved to drink for its own good by a similar cause. Now, with regard to the use its maker intended a clock for, I may say that it departs from its proper nature when it tells the hours wrongly. On the same principle, if I regard the machine of the human body as formed by God for the sake of the motions it usually shows, I may likewise have ground to think that it departs from the order of its nature when the throat is parched and drink does not help to preserve it. Nevertheless I plainly see that this second sense of the term nature is very different from the first. The second is nothing more than a certain denomination, which depends entirely on my thought, and is therefore called extrinsic: by it I compare a sick man and an imperfectly built clock with the idea I have of a healthy man and a well made clock. The first sense of nature means something truly found in things, and so having some truth.

19. To begin this examination, I first observe that mind and body differ vastly in this respect: body, by its nature, is always divisible, while mind is entirely indivisible. For when I consider the mind, that is, when I consider myself only as a thinking thing, I can distinguish no parts in myself. I discern very clearly that I am something absolutely one and entire. The whole mind seems to be united to the whole body; yet when a foot, an arm or any other part is cut off, I am conscious that nothing has been taken away from my mind. Nor can the faculties of willing, perceiving, conceiving and so on properly be called parts of it, since it is one and the same mind that is exercised [all entire] in willing, in perceiving and in conceiving. With corporeal or extended things the very opposite holds. I cannot imagine any of them [however small] that I cannot easily divide in thought, and so I know it to be divisible. This alone would be enough to teach me that the mind, or soul, of man is entirely different from the body, if I had not already learned it on other grounds.

24. And certainly this consideration is of great service. It enables me to recognize the errors to which my nature is liable, and it also makes them easier to avoid or correct. For I know that all my senses more often indicate what is true than what is false in matters relating to the advantage of the body. I can almost always use more than one sense to examine the same object. Besides this, I can use my memory to connect present knowledge with past, and I have my understanding, which has already discovered all the causes of my errors. So I ought no longer to fear that falsity may be found in what the senses present to me every day. And I ought to reject all the doubts of those earlier days as hyperbolical and ridiculous, especially the general uncertainty about sleep, which I could not distinguish from the waking state. For I now find a very marked difference between the two. Our memory can never connect our dreams with one another and with the course of life, as it habitually does with events that occur while we are awake. Indeed, suppose someone appeared to me while I was awake, all of a sudden, and disappeared just as suddenly, as the images I see in sleep do, so that I could not observe where he came from or where he went. I should not without reason consider him a specter or phantom formed in my brain, rather than a real man. But there are objects for which I can determine distinctly the place they come from, the place where they are, and the time at which they appear to me. And I can connect my perception of them, without interruption, with all the other parts of my life. Then I am perfectly sure that I perceive them while I am awake and not in sleep. I ought not to doubt the truth of these presentations in the least, if I have called together all my senses, my memory and my understanding to examine them, and none of these faculties gives a report that conflicts with that of any other. For since God is no deceiver, it necessarily follows that I am not deceived in this. But the necessities of action often oblige us to decide before we have had time for so careful an examination. So it must be confessed that the life of man is often liable to error about individual objects; and we must, in conclusion, acknowledge the weakness of our nature.
